title: Book once and recover an uncertain result
question: A booking request timed out. Is it safe to create another shipment?
definition: Shipment booking creates an external resource linked to the store’s fulfillment intent. Internal order IDs, merchant references, provider order IDs and provider shipment IDs are different identifiers. A timeout means the result is unknown to the caller; it does not prove that the provider failed to create the resource.
why: If Fieldstore retries an unknown booking as a new order, one paid shirt can receive two labels or pickups. A durable booking record, consistent reference and recovery process prevent the interface from treating every network retry as a new business action.
steps: Create one durable fulfillment intent and serialize its booking attempts.
Persist provider identifiers and the request outcome when available.
On uncertainty, reconcile the existing intent before authorizing a new create.
example: ORDER_PLACEHOLDER has one parcel. Booking attempt BOOKING_PLACEHOLDER times out after the synthetic provider creates SHIPMENT_PLACEHOLDER. The next worker looks up and verifies the existing booking by supported references, attaches that provider ID and resumes. It does not manufacture a new merchant reference to bypass the uncertainty.
misconception: Every POST can be retried safely, and passing the same reference guarantees deduplication even if the provider never documents that behavior.
prompt: Implement the agreed book once and recover an uncertain result fixtures using existing conventions. Preserve access, money, stock and retry rules; make no live calls.
exercise: The simulated provider created a shipment but its response was lost. Which next action protects the order?
answer: Keep the booking uncertain and reconcile the existing reference using the provider’s supported lookup or operator review. Reuse a confirmed booking. Do not assume an undocumented idempotency header or duplicate-reference guarantee; create again only after evidence and policy resolve the uncertainty.

details.title: Store the mapping explicitly
details.body: Keep internal order and fulfillment IDs separate from Shiprocket order and shipment IDs. Some API requests require the provider ID rather than the merchant order reference. Save which identifier each operation accepts. Split parcels, when added later, require distinct fulfillment intents rather than overloading one order field.

details.title: Protect the local operation
details.body: Use a uniqueness constraint or transaction-controlled claim so two workers cannot concurrently initiate the same logical booking. Record states such as prepared, requesting, uncertain, booked and manual_review. The network call and provider creation cannot be assumed to share a transaction with the local database.

details.title: Recover with evidence
details.body: A known validation rejection differs from a lost response. Inspect supported provider lookup fields and verify order, parcel and account matches before attaching a result. If evidence is ambiguous, hold the operation for review instead of sending another parcel. Keep correlation IDs and redacted responses; never store credentials in booking payload logs.

title: AWB, labels, manifests and pickup
question: Does generating a label mean the parcel has left the warehouse?
definition: An air waybill number identifies a carrier shipment. A label marks the parcel, a manifest records a handover grouping, and a pickup request asks for collection. These artifacts and actions are related but distinct; none alone proves the courier physically collected the parcel.
why: Fieldstore staff need a sequence they can inspect and resume. Calling later steps with the wrong identifier or treating a printed PDF as shipment movement creates incorrect customer messages and stock records.
steps: Confirm the booked provider shipment and assign an eligible courier/AWB.
Generate the appropriate label and request pickup using documented prerequisites.
Generate or print the manifest and record actual handover separately.
example: The synthetic booking returns a provider shipment ID. Its AWB is assigned; the label becomes ready. Pickup is requested, then a manifest can be generated for the documented eligible shipments. If the pickup request fails, keep the existing booking and AWB and retry or reconcile that step instead of creating another shipment.
misconception: Label-ready, pickup-requested and physically picked-up are the same status.
prompt: Implement the agreed awb, labels, manifests and pickup fixtures using existing conventions. Preserve access, money, stock and retry rules; make no live calls.
exercise: A label PDF exists, but the courier has not collected the parcel. Which customer-facing status is honest?
answer: Prepared or awaiting pickup, according to the store’s status contract. A generated label is not proof of collection. Keep booking, document generation and pickup milestones separate, and move to shipped only when the chosen physical handover evidence is recorded.

Fieldstore’s stock policy deducts on-hand inventory at confirmed shipment/handover, once per allocation; a duplicate pickup event must not deduct stock again.

title: Trust tracking events and reconcile gaps
question: Can a delayed in-transit event undo a delivered shipment?
definition: Tracking integration turns provider observations into the store’s internal shipment timeline. A webhook is an incoming provider notification; polling is a request for the provider’s current record. Authentication, event validation, duplicate handling and transition rules determine whether either observation can change business state.
why: Fieldstore must not accept an unauthenticated request saying an order was delivered. It also must not regress a delivered parcel because an older event arrived late, or assume missing notifications mean no movement occurred.
steps: Authenticate the provider request using its actual documented mechanism.
Persist and validate the event, identifier mapping and transition evidence.
Reconcile gaps or contradictions with an authenticated provider lookup.
example: The fixture receives delivered at 14:00, then an in-transit observation timestamped 10:00. Preserve both for investigation, keep the confirmed delivered state and reconcile if the records conflict. A repeated delivered event must not repeat notifications or inventory effects.
misconception: Every shipping provider signs webhooks with the same HMAC algorithm, and status numbers always increase with progress.
prompt: Implement the agreed trust tracking events and reconcile gaps fixtures using existing conventions. Preserve access, money, stock and retry rules; make no live calls.
exercise: A delivered shipment receives an older in-transit event. What is the safest normal handling?
answer: Record the observation but do not blindly regress the shipment. Check event time, identifier mapping, allowed transitions and any correction semantics; reconcile ambiguous conflicts. Numeric order of provider status codes is not a state machine.

details.title: Use the actual webhook contract

Fieldstore requires a configured strong token for this integration design and checks it on the server. Confirm current account behavior before live use. Do not send credentials in URLs or log header values.

details.title: Validate more than the header

Provider order-status and shipment-status code sets can differ. Unknown values should create a review signal, not be guessed into delivered.

details.title: Handle retries and missing events
details.body: Persist a deduplication key from provider identity when available or a carefully defined event fingerprint. Acknowledge valid accepted notifications according to the provider contract after durable ingestion; Shiprocket documents HTTP 200. Track processing separately. Poll with rate limits and backoff to find stale shipments, and reconcile contradictions without replaying completed effects.

title: Failed delivery, reattempt and return paths
question: Is an undelivered parcel already back in sellable stock?
definition: A non-delivery report records a failed delivery attempt that needs action. A reattempt asks the carrier to try again. Return to origin brings an undelivered parcel back to the sender, while a customer return after delivery is a separate reverse-fulfillment process with its own authorization and tracking.
why: Fieldstore must communicate honestly while respecting courier constraints and customer choices. Reattempt requests, cancellation requests and return initiation are requests or intermediate states, not proof of completed delivery, cancellation or warehouse receipt.
steps: Read the failure reason and confirm the current physical shipment state.
Choose the allowed reattempt, cancellation or return action under policy.
Track the resulting movement to receipt before stock and refund decisions.
example: A synthetic prepaid order reaches out_for_delivery, then undelivered because the customer is unavailable. Staff confirm a reattempt through the approved process. If return-to-origin is initiated instead, the item stays unavailable for resale until physically received and inspected.
misconception: Canceling the store order can always stop a parcel already with the courier.
prompt: Implement the agreed failed delivery, reattempt and return paths fixtures using existing conventions. Preserve access, money, stock and retry rules; make no live calls.
exercise: The courier confirms return-to-origin initiated. Should the shirt immediately become available inventory?
answer: No. RTO initiated indicates a return process, not warehouse receipt or sellable condition. Track the parcel, receive it and inspect it before restocking under policy. Money and refund decisions remain separate from the movement status.

details.title: Use provider-supported actions
details.body: Shiprocket documents NDR actions and account workflows, including reattempt and return-related handling. Supported actions, deadlines and required evidence can vary by courier and case. Do not invent a universal retry count. Validate customer address corrections and minimize personal information in support logs.

details.title: Cancellation has a physical boundary
details.body: Before dispatch, the provider may permit a supported cancellation. After pickup, cancellation may be unavailable or become an interception or return request. Record requested versus confirmed cancellation and check the provider’s current state. Never mark a moving parcel canceled merely because the user pressed a button.

details.title: Keep return types separate
details.body: RTO follows failed forward delivery; a customer return follows delivery and store approval. Reverse pickup needs an authorized return record, eligible items and its own provider references. Track partial returns by item quantity. A carrier-reported return is evidence of movement, while warehouse inspection decides whether the goods are sellable.

title: Inspection, refunds and COD remittance
question: Does delivered mean the store has received the money?
definition: Delivery, payment collection, merchant remittance, refund and inventory are separate business dimensions. Cash on delivery records money collected by a courier; remittance is the later transfer or settlement to the merchant under its arrangement. A return inspection determines item condition, not whether a refund transfer has succeeded.
why: Fieldstore needs to explain a delivered COD order whose remittance is still pending and a returned prepaid shirt whose refund is approved but not processed. One status called complete cannot represent these different facts safely.
steps: Record each dimension using its own evidence and identifiers.
Apply item inspection and refund policy without coupling unrelated statuses.
Reconcile courier collection, remittance and bank evidence before closing money records.
example: A synthetic COD order totals 25000 INR minor units. It is delivered and collection is reported, but the merchant bank has not received remittance. Store those facts separately. Later, a return arrives damaged: record receipt and failed sellability inspection; do not automatically add it to available stock or claim an unprocessed refund succeeded.
misconception: Delivered means paid into the merchant bank; returned means refunded and restocked.
prompt: Implement the agreed inspection, refunds and cod remittance fixtures using existing conventions. Preserve access, money, stock and retry rules; make no live calls.
exercise: A COD parcel is delivered and collection is confirmed, but no remittance is matched. What should staff see?
answer: Delivered, collection confirmed, remittance pending or under reconciliation. Check the provider remittance record, applicable deductions and bank evidence separately. Do not charge again, invent a settlement date, or mark the cash as bank-received solely from tracking.

visual.caption: Synthetic Fieldstore walkthrough: physical delivery, collection, settlement, refund and stock require different evidence. No provider or cloud account is contacted.

details.title: Inspect before restocking
details.body: Record received quantity, condition and disposition. Only sellable units return to available stock, once per authorized receipt. Damaged units may need a separate inventory location or write-off. Refund eligibility follows the stated store policy and applicable obligations; it is not inferred solely from whether the shirt can be resold.

details.title: Handle refunds as operations
details.body: Keep approved amount, currency, method, attempt ID and confirmed result. Prevent duplicate refunds and cap them against the eligible collected amount. A prepaid return may use its payment provider; a COD refund needs an explicitly approved payout method. Never assume shipping software performs every payment operation automatically.

details.title: Reconcile COD rather than guessing
details.body: Match shipment and order references to collection and remittance records, fees, adjustments and bank receipt. Provider plans can have different timing and eligibility, so use current account terms rather than a hard-coded number of days. An advance or remittance entry is not identical to delivery evidence. Investigate unmatched amounts and retain an audit trail.

debugClues: Delivered but cash missing: inspect collection and remittance separately.
Available stock too high: inspect duplicate or uninspected receipts.
Refund says approved forever: inspect its execution attempt and confirmation.

title: Create a trusted payment attempt
question: Which amount and order should hosted checkout receive?
definition: A payment attempt is your durable record of one effort to pay a particular order. The server calculates the payable amount, creates the provider order, and stores their relationship before the browser opens hosted checkout.
why: A checkout popup can collect payment details, but it cannot decide who owns the cart or what the shirt costs. A local attempt record gives a timeout, retry or later webhook something reliable to reconcile.
steps: Authenticate the customer and calculate a fresh quote from trusted records.
Save the attempt and create the matching provider order using server credentials.
Pass the provider order reference and public checkout configuration to the browser.
example: Fieldstore sells blue shirts at 25000 INR minor units, or ₹250 each. Two shirts produce a synthetic 50000-minor-unit quote with no additional charges in this exercise. A browser submitting 1 as the total must still receive the server-calculated amount. Persist internal order FS-1001 and attempt A-1 separately from the provider order reference.
misconception: The checkout amount submitted by the browser is safe because the payment widget is hosted.
prompt: Implement only the agreed server-created payment attempts behavior using existing conventions. Preserve ownership, trusted INR totals and one logical attempt. Use placeholders and provider stubs for this course; isolate optional real-provider code behind an explicit integration boundary.
exercise: The browser submits total=1 for two shirts. Which amount should create the provider order?
answer: Use the authenticated cart and trusted prices to compute 50000 INR minor units, then link the provider order to that internal attempt. Reject or ignore the untrusted total under the API contract. Hosted checkout does not replace server pricing.

title: Verify payment before fulfillment
question: What should happen when the browser says success but the backend is uncertain?

why: Customers close tabs and events arrive late or repeatedly. The backend must produce the same payment effect from consistent verified evidence, regardless of which message arrives first.
steps: Receive checkout proof or an event without trusting its claimed outcome.
Verify through the provider-supported mechanism and match order, amount and currency.
Persist the verified transition once; reconcile uncertain or conflicting evidence.
example: Fieldstore displays “Payment received; confirming your order” after the popup returns. A-1 remains pending verification. Staff see the attempt reference and a reconciliation action, not an instruction to charge again. A verified captured payment for the expected 50000 INR amount can confirm allocation; a duplicate event does not allocate twice.

title: Capture, refunds and settlement are different
question: When does a successful payment become money in the merchant bank?
definition: Authorization, capture, refund and settlement describe different money movements. Capture confirms collection according to the payment method and provider configuration. Settlement transfers eligible provider-held funds to the merchant bank. A refund is a separate request to return money.
why: Combining these concepts in one paid flag hides missing funds and failed refunds. Customer order status needs payment evidence, while finance needs a reconciliation ledger that includes fees, adjustments, refunds and bank transfers.
steps: Confirm the capture behavior that applies to the selected payment method and account.
Create an authorized, bounded refund operation with its own durable reference.
Reconcile captured money, refunds, fees and settlements against provider and bank evidence.
example: A Fieldstore shirt payment of 25000 INR minor units is captured today. The order may be paid while settlement is still pending. A later return creates refund R-1; the original payment stays historically captured while refund status advances separately. Stock is restocked only after a sellable-item inspection, not because the refund API accepted a request.
misconception: Captured means the bank has already received the merchant payout, and refund accepted means the customer has received funds.
prompt: Implement only the agreed capture refund and settlement records behavior using existing conventions. Preserve refund authorization, bounded INR amounts and independent stock decisions. Use placeholders and provider stubs for this course; isolate optional real-provider code behind an explicit integration boundary.
exercise: A payment is captured but its settlement is pending. Should checkout be marked unpaid?
answer: No. Preserve the verified captured payment and track settlement separately. Investigate delayed settlement through provider and bank records. A refund also needs its own state and reconciliation; changing the payment history to failed would destroy useful evidence.

title: Choose the message and prove the sender
question: What makes a receipt different from a marketing campaign?
definition: A transactional notification supports an account or purchase action, such as verification, password recovery, a receipt or a shipment update. Marketing promotes an offer. Their purposes, preferences and delivery policies should be explicit before choosing a template or sending provider.
why: A reliable notification system starts with the correct recipient and reason. Mixing promotional content into sensitive account messages can confuse preferences, while an unverified sender domain can prevent even a useful receipt from reaching the customer.
steps: Classify the intent and select the correct authorized recipient and template.
Configure a verified sender identity and document channel-specific preferences.
Preview sanitized template data and inspect delivery authentication evidence.
example: Fieldstore needs a receipt for order FS-1001 and a separate newsletter invitation. The receipt contains the purchased blue shirt, 25000 INR minor-unit total and a safe order link. A password-reset template contains a short-lived recovery link from the auth system, not the password. The newsletter follows its own subscription preference.
misconception: An API key lets any From address send trusted mail, and every customer message is marketing.
prompt: Implement only the agreed transactional message templates and sender identity behavior using existing conventions. Preserve trusted recipients, purpose-specific preferences and redacted recovery links. Use placeholders and provider stubs for this course; isolate optional real-provider code behind an explicit integration boundary.
exercise: Which design separates account safety from promotional preference?
answer: Keep password recovery and order notifications tied to their specific service purpose, and maintain a distinct marketing preference. Use the auth system for recovery-token lifecycle and a verified sender domain. Do not assume one opt-in flag covers every jurisdiction or channel.

title: Queue one notification intent
question: How do five order events produce one confirmation message?
definition: A notification intent records the business decision to send a particular message. A queue asks a worker to deliver that intent. The durable intent key identifies the message across duplicate events, worker retries and uncertain provider responses.
why: Retries are essential, but each retry should not become a fresh customer message. A unique database constraint and provider-specific retry mechanism protect the intended effect when the worker crashes between sending and saving the response.
steps: Write one durable intent with the order transition, preferably through an outbox.
Let a worker claim it and use the same provider idempotency identity for retries.
Store provider results; investigate uncertainty before sending a new logical message.
example: Five replayed order-confirmed events reference FS-1001. Fieldstore derives intent order_receipt:FS-1001:v1 once. A Resend send attempt times out; the worker retries that same request with the same idempotency key within the documented window. The durable ledger still prevents a duplicate receipt when an old order event reappears next week.
misconception: A queue guarantees each email sends exactly once forever.
prompt: Implement only the agreed queued notification intents and retry handling behavior using existing conventions. Preserve one message intent, bounded retries and a durable send ledger. Use placeholders and provider stubs for this course; isolate optional real-provider code behind an explicit integration boundary.
exercise: A receipt event is replayed after the provider idempotency window. What prevents a duplicate?
answer: The application notification ledger must remember the completed business intent beyond the provider window. A durable unique key handles repeated events. For uncertain old sends, reconcile rather than blindly retrying with a new key. A provider key is useful but is not permanent business history.

details.title: The specific provider limit

details.title: Crash-aware delivery
details.body: The intent and queue/outbox record belong in one database transaction. A worker crash after external acceptance leaves an uncertain send, not proof of failure. Track attempts, bounded backoff and a review path; prevent concurrent workers from claiming independent intents for the same receipt.

debugClues: New random keys on every retry defeat duplicate protection.
A sent API request without its saved response may already have produced mail.
An outbox entry missing after order commit reveals a split transaction.

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX notification_intent_once
ON notification_intents (order_id, kind, recipient_id, channel, template_version);

title: Accepted, delivered or failed?
question: What does the provider know about the customer receiving a message?
definition: A delivery state describes observed progress after a notification request. Provider acceptance means the request entered the provider system. Later evidence may show delivery, delay, bounce or failure. Even a delivery receipt is not proof that a person read and understood the message.
why: Customers need accurate communication and staff need actionable failures. Treating every accepted request as delivered hides bad addresses, blocked senders, SMS carrier problems and retry storms that harm reputation or cost money.
steps: Record the provider message reference and initial accepted or queued state.
Authenticate callbacks and map them to documented channel-specific states.
Apply bounce, suppression, preference and retry rules; reconcile missing events.
example: Resend accepts Fieldstore receipt N-1, then reports a permanent bounce. The order remains confirmed but its notification needs attention. A Twilio SMS may be sent to a carrier and later become undelivered. Staff see a redacted reason and contact workflow; they do not repeatedly resend the same failed message every minute.
misconception: HTTP 200 from an email or SMS send API proves the person received the message.
prompt: Implement only the agreed email and SMS delivery tracking behavior using existing conventions. Preserve authenticated callbacks, separate order state and privacy-aware failure handling. Use placeholders and provider stubs for this course; isolate optional real-provider code behind an explicit integration boundary.
exercise: Email is accepted, then a permanent bounce arrives. What should change?
answer: Update notification delivery evidence and apply the appropriate suppression or address-correction workflow. Keep payment and order status unchanged. A permanent failure does not become success by retrying the same invalid destination repeatedly.

visual.caption: Trace email and SMS delivery tracking: each boundary needs an input, a rule, a result and evidence.

details.title: Read the precise event meaning
details.body: Resend distinguishes sent, delivered-to-mail-server, delayed, bounced and failed events. Twilio distinguishes queued, sent, delivered, failed and undelivered SMS states. Avoid converting every provider word into a single boolean or assuming read receipts exist for ordinary SMS.

details.title: Authenticate and minimize
details.body: Resend webhook verification uses its signing secret and raw payload. Twilio recommends its maintained signature-validation helpers for evolving callback parameters. Retain only necessary event evidence, restrict staff access and redact email addresses, phone numbers and reset links in logs.

debugClues: No callback may mean wrong callback configuration, not successful delivery.
A hard bounce and a temporary delay require different responses.
Matching by email address alone can attach an event to the wrong message.

title: Follow DNS, HTTPS and callbacks
question: Which layer fails before the application receives a request?
definition: DNS connects a hostname to a network destination. HTTPS uses TLS to protect the connection and authenticate the server hostname. A callback URL names the endpoint another system should contact; it must be reachable from that system, not merely from your browser.
why: A correct handler cannot answer traffic that never reaches it. Distinguishing name resolution, TLS, routing and application behavior prevents random code changes when the real problem is a hostname, certificate, port or provider callback setting.
steps: Resolve the intended hostname and identify the destination and environment.
Check TLS hostname validity and route reachability before application logic.
Match the exact callback URL, method and provider restrictions to the handler.
example: Fieldstore local pages run at http://127.0.0.1:3000. That address points to each caller’s own computer, so a payment provider cannot use it to reach this app. The local exercise passes synthetic signed fixtures to a verifier. A future optional provider test would need an explicitly approved, supported reachable endpoint and test-mode credentials.
misconception: Changing a callback to localhost makes it reachable from every provider.
prompt: Implement only the agreed DNS HTTPS and callback routing behavior using existing conventions. Preserve correct environment, valid TLS and authenticated callbacks. Use placeholders and provider stubs for this course; isolate optional real-provider code behind an explicit integration boundary.
exercise: The browser opens a local page but the external provider cannot deliver its webhook. What explains the difference?
answer: Loopback refers to the machine making the request. The provider is not running on your laptop. Diagnose reachability and the provider’s callback restrictions; do not disable authentication or publish the whole course to solve a synthetic exercise.

details.title: Keep names and origins straight
details.body: store.example.test and api.example.test are different hosts. A path such as /webhooks/payment selects a handler on a host. A callback configuration must match the intended environment; a test event reaching a production handler is a dangerous routing mistake.

title: CORS, cookies and CSRF solve different problems
question: Why can an API client succeed while a browser request fails?
definition: An origin is the combination of scheme, hostname and port. CORS governs whether browser JavaScript can read certain cross-origin responses. Authentication identifies the caller; authorization permits an action. CSRF defenses protect cookie-authenticated state changes from unwanted cross-site requests.
why: An API client does not enforce the browser’s CORS rules. A broad CORS change can hide the original error while leaving access unsafe. Cookies and CSRF need explicit design even when a browser request eventually succeeds.
steps: Inspect the browser request, preflight and response headers before changing configuration.
Check whether the expected session cookie or authorization credential was sent and verified.
Apply a narrow origin policy and maintained CSRF protection to protected mutations.
example: A local Fieldstore UI on port 3000 calls an API on port 4000. The preflight lacks an allowed-origin response, so JavaScript cannot read the result. After CORS is fixed, a request for another customer’s order still returns 403. Those are separate outcomes: the browser boundary now works, and the ownership rule correctly rejects access.
misconception: Allowing every origin authenticates the caller and fixes authorization.
prompt: Implement only the agreed browser origin cookies and CSRF boundaries behavior using existing conventions. Preserve specific allowed origins, verified sessions and per-resource authorization. Use placeholders and provider stubs for this course; isolate optional real-provider code behind an explicit integration boundary.
exercise: The preflight succeeds but customer A receives 403 for customer B’s order. What should be changed?
answer: Nothing should relax the ownership check. CORS permission is not permission to read that order. Confirm the session, actor and requested resource, then preserve the rejection. Use a valid owned order to test a successful application request.

visual.caption: Trace browser origin cookies and CSRF boundaries: each boundary needs an input, a rule, a result and evidence.

details.title: Cookie details matter
details.body: Secure limits cookie transport to secure contexts; HttpOnly prevents script reading the cookie but not all misuse. SameSite influences cross-site sending and is not identical to same-origin. Use the authentication framework’s supported cookie settings and examine actual browser storage and request headers.

details.title: Fix the right boundary
details.body: Credentialed CORS cannot use wildcard Allow-Origin. Allow only intended origins and the required methods/headers. CORS is not a replacement for CSRF protection or authorization. Prefer maintained framework defenses and validate every protected state-changing request on the server.

debugClues: A browser console CORS error can hide an underlying application error.
A missing cookie may be origin, SameSite, Secure or credentials configuration.
A correct 403 is a permission result, not proof of a network failure.

implementation.code:
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://127.0.0.1:3000
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Vary: Origin
implementation.note: Illustrative local allowed-origin response, not a complete middleware configuration. Preflight methods/headers, session checks and CSRF defenses remain required.

completionChecks: Diagnose preflight and ownership failures separately.

title: Protect expensive and untrusted boundaries
question: Which checks still matter after login succeeds?
definition: Application hardening places checks where untrusted input becomes a query, rendered page, file, privileged operation or expensive provider call. Login is only the beginning: each operation needs appropriate data handling, ownership checks, resource limits and auditable credentials.
why: A customer can submit hostile text, guess another order, upload unsafe content or exhaust a paid endpoint. Useful AI instructions name the exact boundary and expected rejection.
steps: Map input to its dangerous use: query, HTML, upload, resource or external request.
Apply maintained protections and narrowly scoped access before costly work.
Review dependencies, scan for secrets and verify representative abuse cases.
example: Fieldstore accepts a return note and photo. The server verifies that the customer owns the return, limits file size and permitted formats, checks content rather than trusting the filename, and stores evidence privately. Staff see safely rendered note text. A rate limit prevents one account from generating unlimited shipping quotes.
misconception: Escaping one field or hiding an admin button makes the whole endpoint secure.
prompt: Implement only the agreed input authorization and resource hardening behavior using existing conventions. Preserve object ownership, safe data handling and bounded external costs. Use placeholders and provider stubs for this course; isolate optional real-provider code behind an explicit integration boundary.
exercise: A customer changes orderId to another buyer’s order after login. Which rule must stop the request?
answer: Server-side resource authorization must reject it before returning data or causing an effect. A random-looking ID, CORS header or hidden button is not an access policy. Test the direct request with two customers and record the denied result.

visual.caption: Trace input authorization and resource hardening: each boundary needs an input, a rule, a result and evidence.

details.title: Different attacks need different controls
details.body: Use parameterized database queries rather than SQL string concatenation. Render untrusted text through safe framework output and sanitize intentionally allowed HTML. Authorize every object access. Validate uploads by allowlisted type, size and content, use generated storage names, and avoid executable public storage.

details.title: Service identity and maintenance
details.body: Authenticate server-to-server calls with the provider-supported mechanism and scoped server-only credentials. Apply rate limits and timeouts before expensive work. Review dependency advisories and lockfile changes; secret scanning helps find leaks but cannot prove absence. Revoke exposed credentials, investigate use, and update dependent services.

debugClues: A 403 missing only on direct API calls exposes UI-only authorization.
A.jpg suffix does not prove the uploaded bytes are a safe image.
A secret removed from the latest file may remain valid or in Git history.

title: Build an evidence trail for the store
question: How can one failed checkout be followed across components?
definition: Observability connects structured events, measurements and request traces so you can explain what the system did. A correlation ID links one business operation across the request handler, database work, queue and provider adapter without requiring customer secrets in every log.
why: A generic 500 error says little about whether money moved or inventory was reserved. Useful evidence narrows the fault, measures user impact and supports a safe recovery decision rather than repeated speculative retries.
steps: Assign operation and correlation identifiers at trusted boundaries.
Record structured outcomes and measure latency, errors, backlog and provider failures.
Alert on actionable symptoms with an owner, evidence link and recovery procedure.
example: Fieldstore checkout FS-1001 returns a timeout. Logs show quote accepted, reservation committed and provider request sent, but no provider result recorded. The trace stops at the adapter. A metric shows three uncertain attempts, not three confirmed failed payments. Staff investigate those references without logging card details, full addresses or credentials.
misconception: Logging every request body gives the best debugging evidence.
prompt: Implement only the agreed structured operational evidence behavior using existing conventions. Preserve correlated IDs, redacted data and observable business outcomes. Use placeholders and provider stubs for this course; isolate optional real-provider code behind an explicit integration boundary.
exercise: Which log entry best helps investigate a payment timeout safely?
answer: Record the operation/correlation ID, safe internal and provider references, stage, duration, outcome and redacted error category. Do not log secrets or full payment/customer payloads. A missing response should be labeled uncertain until provider evidence resolves it.

visual.caption: Trace structured operational evidence: each boundary needs an input, a rule, a result and evidence.

details.title: Use the appropriate signal
details.body: Logs explain events, metrics summarize behavior, and traces follow work across boundaries. OpenTelemetry provides shared concepts for these signals; the course does not require installing a paid monitoring service. Synthetic records are enough to practice joining evidence.

details.title: Privacy and cost are design inputs
details.body: Allowlist useful log fields and sanitize untrusted strings. Avoid credentials, session tokens, full message bodies and unnecessary personal data. Restrict retention and access. Watch log volume, high-cardinality labels and tracing overhead so investigation tooling does not create unexpected cost.

debugClues: Different IDs at each layer prevent one checkout from being traced.
Success-only logs hide the timeouts that need investigation most.
An alert with no owner or action becomes background noise.

title: Recover workers, connections and stale caches
question: Why can adding more workers make a backlog worse?
definition: An operational bottleneck is the constrained resource preventing useful work from completing. Queue backlog, database connection exhaustion, slow queries and stale cache entries can look like the same slow store, but each needs different evidence and recovery behavior.
why: Blindly increasing retries or worker count can multiply pressure on a failing dependency. A safe recovery fixes the cause, limits traffic, preserves pending work and verifies business effects before replaying a backlog.
steps: Compare queue age, worker outcomes, connection use and query latency.
Repair the cause and choose bounded concurrency, retry and cache policies.
Replay a small safe sample, then verify unique effects and recovery metrics.
example: Fieldstore has twenty shipment workers but a small database pool. Each worker holds a connection while waiting for a provider response, so checkout requests time out too. Limit concurrent work, release connections before slow external calls and inspect transaction scope. Failed jobs stay visible; repeatedly failing payloads move to a review/dead-letter path.
misconception: A dead-letter queue fixes the failed jobs automatically.
prompt: Implement only the agreed worker backlog and database recovery behavior using existing conventions. Preserve bounded concurrency, preserved jobs and idempotent business effects. Use placeholders and provider stubs for this course; isolate optional real-provider code behind an explicit integration boundary.
exercise: Workers are retrying rapidly while the database has no free connections. What should happen first?
answer: Reduce the pressure and inspect connection ownership, long transactions and slow queries before increasing workers. Preserve jobs and diagnose the dependency. Once repaired, replay a bounded sample with duplicate protection and compare queue age, errors and business records.

visual.caption: Trace worker backlog and database recovery: each boundary needs an input, a rule, a result and evidence.

details.title: Dead-letter means investigate
details.body: A dead-letter path isolates repeatedly unsuccessful work for review. Amazon SQS documents this pattern; exact retry and ordering behavior depends on the queue. Fix payload or dependency problems, preserve evidence, and redrive intentionally rather than looping all failed jobs forever.

details.title: Cache and database evidence
details.body: PostgreSQL exposes activity statistics for current connections and work. A stale product cache may explain old display data, but checkout must still use authoritative pricing and stock rules. Invalidate or version the affected cache deliberately; avoid flushing everything before understanding the source of truth.

debugClues: Connection count rising with worker count suggests a shared capacity limit.
Queue age grows even when request latency appears healthy.
A restarted worker can repeat an external call whose prior response was lost.

implementation.code:
SELECT state, wait_event_type, count(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = current_database()
GROUP BY state, wait_event_type;
implementation.note: Read-only diagnostic shape. Results require sufficient database privileges; inspect aggregates before exposing query text that might contain private values.

title: Restore data and reconcile external reality
question: What does a database restore fail to undo?
definition: Recovery restores usable service and trustworthy business state after failure. A backup is a saved recovery input, not proof that recovery works. Recovery point objective describes tolerable data loss; recovery time objective describes tolerable downtime. Both need business agreement and a measured drill.
why: Restoring yesterday’s database cannot undo a payment captured or parcel booked this morning. Code rollback, database recovery, stored files, provider records and credentials have separate scopes. Reconciliation connects them before normal processing resumes.
steps: Define recovery objectives and inventory every required data source and secret reference.
Restore into an isolated environment with real external effects disabled.
Reconcile operations since the recovery point and verify invariants before reopening work.
example: Fieldstore restores a database copy missing A-1 and shipment S-1. The provider still has the captured payment and booked parcel. The recovery team compares stable references, reconstructs or flags missing local records and blocks fresh duplicate charges or bookings. Product photos and private return files need their own backup/restore coverage.
misconception: Rolling back code or restoring the database reverses provider side effects.
prompt: Implement only the agreed restore drills and business reconciliation behavior using existing conventions. Preserve isolated recovery, preserved audit evidence and no duplicate external effects. Use placeholders and provider stubs for this course; isolate optional real-provider code behind an explicit integration boundary.
exercise: A restored database says unpaid, but the provider has a captured payment. What is the next safe action?
answer: Reconcile the trusted provider record to the intended order and rebuild or review the missing local attempt. Do not charge again based solely on the restored state. Preserve an audit record and verify amount, currency, ownership and stock decisions before resuming fulfillment.

details.title: Operate within budgets

A rollback should be schema-compatible and cannot reverse external effects; use explicit compensating workflows and reconcile their results.

Missing object files expose an incomplete backup scope.

title: Capstone: identity, product and cart
question: Can you trace a customer action without losing its owner or price?
definition: The Fieldstore capstone connects one purchase. Verified identity and public product information become a private cart. Each stage names the actor, records, permission, service, failure and evidence.
why: The next step inherits the previous step’s assumptions. A cart with the wrong owner or an untrusted price makes later payment and shipping logic unsafe even when every provider integration appears to work.
steps: Verify a synthetic signup/login and derive customer identity on the server.
Read an active blue-shirt variant priced at 25000 INR minor units.
Add quantity to that customer’s durable cart and confirm it survives reload.
example: Customer A buys one blue shirt from Fieldstore. Customer B is a separate test identity. A may browse the public catalog, but only A can mutate A’s cart. A forged profile role does not confer staff access. Cart display is provisional; checkout will calculate a fresh trusted quote and reserve stock under the documented rule.
misconception: A completed signup screen proves every future session is valid and every cart is owned.
prompt: Implement only the agreed Fieldstore signup product and cart flow behavior using existing conventions. Preserve verified customer identity, private cart ownership and authoritative prices. Use placeholders and provider stubs for this course; isolate optional real-provider code behind an explicit integration boundary.
exercise: Customer B sends A’s cart ID with B’s valid session. Should Add to cart succeed?
answer: No. A valid session establishes B’s identity, not access to A’s cart. Deny the operation without revealing private cart details or changing records. Then demonstrate the successful request with A and verify the saved cart after a reload.

details.title: One explicit teaching model
details.body: Fieldstore uses one warehouse, prepaid INR orders and one blue-shirt variant at 25000 minor units. Shipping is zero and tax is treated as included in the synthetic quote. These are exercise assumptions, not tax advice or a production pricing specification.

details.title: A contract at every handoff
details.body: Record actor, input, output, permission and failure for signup, product and cart. Use placeholders for auth and database services. An optional real integration needs its own provider tests; passing the local capstone proves understanding of this model only.

debugClues: An expired session should produce a safe reauthentication path.
Public product reads do not make cart or order rows public.
A UI-only quantity change disappears on reload if persistence is missing.

title: Capstone: checkout, payment and order
question: How does one last shirt become one paid order?
definition: Checkout converts a cart into a priced order intent and a protected stock claim. Payment verification confirms the financial result for that intent. Order confirmation preserves the purchased item and price snapshot. These are connected transitions, not one browser-controlled paid flag.
why: Two customers can want the last unit while payment notifications arrive repeatedly. The store needs atomic stock rules and durable operation identities so that money and inventory stay consistent under concurrency and retries.
steps: Calculate the trusted quote and atomically claim the remaining unit for one checkout.
Create or recover the logical payment attempt and verify provider evidence.
Confirm the order snapshot and allocation once; queue downstream work durably.
example: Fieldstore begins with onHand 1, reserved 0, available 1. A and B compete. One checkout reserves 1; the other receives unavailable. A’s browser says success, but fulfillment waits for verified capture of 25000 INR minor units. The captured event is replayed: confirmed allocation stays 1, and onHand remains 1 until physical shipment.
misconception: Payment confirmation should deduct physical inventory again after checkout reserved it.
prompt: Implement only the agreed Fieldstore checkout payment and order transitions behavior using existing conventions. Preserve one last-unit reservation, trusted 25000 INR amount and duplicate-safe capture. Use placeholders and provider stubs for this course; isolate optional real-provider code behind an explicit integration boundary.
exercise: After reservation and verified capture, what inventory values fit this teaching model?
answer: Keep onHand 1 and reserved 1, so available 0. Payment confirms the allocation but does not consume physical stock a second time. Shipment later changes onHand and reserved together to 0. A duplicate capture must leave those counts unchanged.

details.title: Independent dimensions
details.body: The capstone separates order state, payment state, reservation state and shipment state. The payment can be captured while shipping is pending; a parcel can later be delivered while merchant settlement is pending. Customer and staff views should explain these dimensions honestly.

details.title: Failure recovery before convenience
details.body: An unpaid reservation may expire under policy. If capture arrives after release, route the case through an explicit stock-check/refund review rather than inventing inventory. Preserve payment evidence and operation references. Repeated clicks and events must recover the same logical effects.

debugClues: Both shoppers winning exposes a non-atomic stock check/update.
Two order-confirmation jobs from one event expose a missing uniqueness rule.
A late failure event must not regress verified captured payment.

title: Capstone: shipment, tracking, return and refund
question: Can the journey finish without erasing its history?
definition: Fulfillment connects booking, physical shipment and delivery. Returns reverse the product journey; refunds return an approved amount. Separate references and permissions preserve evidence during recovery.
why: A timed-out booking may already exist, a late tracking event may be stale, and a returned item may be unsellable. Separating the records prevents duplicate labels, negative inventory, premature restocking and repeated refunds.
steps: Book or recover the existing shipment and confirm physical handoff before consuming stock.
Map authenticated tracking evidence without regressing a completed state.
Authorize the return, inspect the received item and reconcile the bounded refund independently.
example: Shipment booking S-1 times out, but provider evidence shows it exists. Fieldstore reuses S-1 instead of booking again. At confirmed handoff, onHand and reserved each decrease from 1 to 0. After delivery, A requests a return. Receipt enters quarantine; a sellable inspection restores 1 available unit. Refund R-1 is tracked to provider completion separately.
misconception: A return request means the item is already sellable stock and the customer has received a refund.
prompt: Implement only the agreed Fieldstore shipment return and refund recovery behavior using existing conventions. Preserve unique shipment intent, inspected restock and bounded authorized refund. Use placeholders and provider stubs for this course; isolate optional real-provider code behind an explicit integration boundary.
exercise: A booking call times out and the provider shows shipment S-1 for FS-1001. What should the worker do?
answer: Link and recover the existing S-1 after matching order and package evidence. Do not create a duplicate booking. Booking alone does not prove physical shipment. Continue tracking, return inspection and refund state changes with their own evidence and permissions.

visual.caption: Trace Fieldstore shipment return and refund recovery: each boundary needs an input, a rule, a result and evidence.

details.title: Provider details remain explicit
details.body: A shipping aggregator and courier can expose different identifiers and status vocabularies. Use the provider’s actual authentication, webhook and recovery features. The capstone invents no API endpoint and assumes no universal sandbox or signature scheme; its fixtures model the business boundary.

details.title: Finish with an evidence pack
details.body: Show the actor, records, permission, service, failure and verification for all ten stages. Include unauthorized access, expired credentials, last-unit competition, duplicate payment evidence and shipping timeout. Record what ran locally and what a future provider test would still need to prove.

debugClues: A duplicate label can reveal a blind retry after an uncertain booking.
Delivered followed by an older in-transit event must not regress delivery.
Refund accepted and item inspected are separate evidence checkpoints.
